clue.text: Doctor behind State conscription

parts.note: DR is the standard abbreviation for doctor
aft is the nautical word for at the back

explanation.surface: A doctor trailing behind some government programme of compulsory military service.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Behind' looks like it positions the doctor, but here it simply supplies its own synonym, placed after DR.
explanation.definitionFit: The draft is the usual American name for compulsory call-up into the armed forces by the government.

clue.text: Those entitled to levies including game

indicators.note: including means holding inside, so one word goes within the other

parts.note: dues are charges or fees levied
chess is a board game

explanation.surface: Some people have a right to collect taxes, game included.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Those entitled to levies' reads as one phrase about tax rights, but the definition stops at 'entitled': people who bear a title.
explanation.definitionFit: Duchesses hold a noble title, so they are literally entitled, people bearing a rank.

clue.text: It flowed for Burns a short distance forward

parts.note: taken as written
FT, a foot, is a short distance
on means forward, as in moving on

explanation.surface: A stream that moved a little way ahead for the poet Burns.
explanation.walkthrough: Robert Burns wrote 'Flow gently, sweet Afton', about a river in Ayrshire, Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: The Afton Water is the Scottish river Burns addressed in his song, so it flowed for him in verse.

clue.text: A valued servant accra accumulated 23
Animal without associate. Hard cheese? Not at all

indicators.note: without is used in its old sense of outside, so one word wraps round the other

parts.note: a cat is a common animal
an associate of a club or society is a member

explanation.surface: An animal left with no friend, and someone grumbling 'hard cheese' at its bad luck.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hard cheese' is a British idiom for bad luck, but read literally it describes a cheese; this one is famously soft, hence 'Not at all'.
explanation.definitionFit: Camembert is a soft, runny French cheese, the very opposite of a hard one, which the question mark signals.

clue.text: This ark contains vehicles or fish

indicators.note: This plus the next word makes a longer phrase, so the answer is that phrase with the next word taken off

parts.note: a car park is a place that holds motor vehicles
taken as written

explanation.surface: Noah's ark carrying vehicles, or perhaps fish.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'This' plus 'ark' together: the answer followed by ARK makes CAR PARK, a place that contains vehicles.
explanation.definitionFit: The carp is a common freshwater fish.

clue.text: New MP got let in for dissolution before a fresh deal

indicators.note: new signals the following letters are made over in a new order

parts.note: the fodder taken as written

explanation.surface: A newly elected MP is admitted as Parliament dissolves ahead of a new political settlement.
explanation.walkthrough: Dissolution looks like the end of a parliament, but here it means melting down; 'in the melting pot' is said of things being reshaped.
explanation.definitionFit: A melting pot is where things are melted down and reformed, a state of flux before a new arrangement.

clue.text: Evolutionary development < of a dumb worker, say?

indicators.note: say asks us to speak the phrase and hear the word it makes

parts.note: dumb means mute, and the worker is the crossword's usual insect worker

explanation.surface: A worker that cannot speak, as a quirky product of evolution.
explanation.walkthrough: A worker is often an ANT in crosswords. The stray '<' in the clue is a printing blemish.
explanation.definitionFit: A mutant is an organism changed by genetic mutation, a development on which evolution acts.

clue.text: Very loud, late cue bungled but netting results

indicators.note: but in its old sense of outside, so the scrambled letters sit round the first piece
something bungled is botched and messed up, so the letters come out in a new order

parts.note: the fodder taken as written
FF, fortissimo, is the musical marking for very loud

explanation.surface: An actor bungles a late cue very loudly, yet still gets the result needed.
explanation.walkthrough: The rearranged LATE CUE goes round FF.
explanation.definitionFit: Something effectual produces the intended effect, so it is succeeding in gaining results.

clue.text: Queen Mab's wagon 'The s. of the smallest spider's web"

definitions.text: Queen Mab's wagon 'The s. of the smallest spider's web"

parts.note: surface reading: the fairy queen's tiny carriage as described in Romeo and Juliet

parts.words: 'The s. of the smallest spider's web"
parts.note: setter's reading: supply the missing word, the s. being the plural ending that follows it

explanation.walkthrough: Mercutio's Queen Mab speech says of her wagon: 'Her traces, of the smallest spider's web'. The 's.' shows the plural ending is already given.
explanation.definitionFit: Traces are the straps joining a horse to a carriage, and Mab's are made of spider's web.

clue.text: Dramatic murder scene

parts.note: surface reading: the setting of some gripping, theatrical killing
setter's reading: the scene of the murder in a famous drama, T. S. Eliot's verse play about Thomas Becket

explanation.walkthrough: Eliot's play is 'Murder in the Cathedral', about the killing of Archbishop Becket at Canterbury in 1170.
explanation.definitionFit: The play's title names the building where Becket was struck down, so it is literally the scene of a dramatised murder.

clue.text: It's rum poor l-Fatima losing a thousand

indicators.note: poor suggests a shabby, disordered state, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: a stray mark in the scanned newspaper text, taken as padding

indicators.note: losing says something is taken away, here the Roman numeral for a thousand

parts.note: the name taken as written
M is the Roman numeral for a thousand

explanation.surface: Someone pitying poor Fatima, perhaps after a drink of rum.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove M from FATIMA, then rearrange what is left. The stray 'l-' before Fatima is a printing blemish in the scanned page.
explanation.definitionFit: Tafia is a cheap rum distilled from sugar-cane molasses, made in the West Indies.

clue.text: "The way of an eagle" for this man'?'

parts.note: the erne is the sea eagle, a crossword favourite
ST, short for street, is a way

explanation.surface: A quotation about an eagle's way of flying, offered as the motto of some man.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation echoes Proverbs ('the way of an eagle in the air') and the title of a popular novel by Ethel M. Dell. The definition is just a man's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Ernest is a man's first name, which is all 'this man' with its question mark asks for.

clue.text: New as a clean pin, it's the tops

indicators.note: something new has been remade, so these letters come in a fresh order

parts.note: the fodder taken as written

explanation.surface: Something as new as a clean pin, praised as simply the best.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase 'new as a pin' (meaning brand new) is the disguise; 'New' is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A pinnacle is the highest point, so it is colloquially the tops, the very best.

clue.text: 'Endowment for supporting women?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a fund set up to support a cause
second meaning: a corset or girdle, a women's undergarment

explanation.walkthrough: 'Supporting women' reads like a charity, but it means physical support: a foundation garment.
explanation.definitionFit: A foundation is both an endowed institution and the dated term for a corset or girdle that shapes the figure.

clue.text: Lumpers employed on board?

parts.note: surface reading: dockers (lumpers is an old word for them) loading cargo aboard a ship
setter's reading: things that lift lumps of sugar, used at the table, the board

explanation.walkthrough: Lumpers were dock labourers, and 'on board' points to a ship; but board also means a dining table, where lumps of sugar are served.
explanation.definitionFit: Sugar tongs pick up sugar lumps at the table, so they are playfully the lumpers used at the board.

clue.text: In hard times hard facts were his solace

definitions.text: In hard times hard facts were his solace

parts.note: surface reading: someone who in difficult days took comfort in plain realities
setter's reading: the fact-obsessed schoolmaster in Dickens's novel Hard Times

explanation.walkthrough: Hard Times is a Dickens novel; Thomas Gradgrind opens it demanding 'Now, what I want is, Facts.'
explanation.definitionFit: Gradgrind is the character who lives by facts alone, and his name now means a cold, fact-bound person.

clue.text: The pudding's no good

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a stiff boiled pudding
second meaning: slang for useless or worthless

explanation.walkthrough: Plum duff is a British steamed or boiled pudding with dried fruit; a duff idea is a bad one.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both a heavy boiled dessert and a slang adjective for something faulty.

clue.text: Machine regulators essential lor sortie old carriages

parts.note: a scanning misreading of 'for', taken as padding joining the definition to the wordplay
a sortie is a flight, and to fly is to make one
wheels is slang for a vehicle, here old-fashioned carriages

explanation.surface: A list of parts needed for an outing in old horse-drawn carriages.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Essential for' joins definition to wordplay. A fly was also a light horse-drawn carriage, which helps the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: A flywheel is a heavy wheel that smooths out a machine's speed, so flywheels regulate machinery.

clue.text: One politician's finished, as threatened

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one
MP, Member of Parliament, is a politician
something finished has ended

explanation.surface: A politician's career is over, just as had been threatened.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that impended loomed or hung over, as a danger that was threatened.

clue.text: .Littlewood writer

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a little wood, a thicket, an old dialect sense
second meaning: the playwright George Bernard ...

explanation.walkthrough: Littlewood looks like Joan Littlewood, the theatre director, which points towards playwrights; split it, and it is a small wood.
explanation.definitionFit: A shaw is an archaic word for a small wood or copse, and Shaw is the Irish dramatist.

clue.text: Tell your friend without ceremony

parts.note: to tell someone something is to inform them
an ally is a friend on your side

explanation.surface: Advice to share news with a friend casually, not formally.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something informally means doing it casually, without formality or ritual.

clue.text: Heard in church as well as in Sunday School

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a Bible reading given aloud during a service
second meaning: a period of teaching given to the children

explanation.walkthrough: Both halves point to church life, but one is a reading and the other a class.
explanation.definitionFit: A lesson is both a scripture reading in a service and a unit of instruction in a class.

clue.text: Soldier at the front knows the drill

definitions.text: Soldier at the front knows the drill

parts.note: surface reading: a veteran in the front line, who knows what to do
setter's reading: a soldier placed in front of the ranks as a model in parade-ground drill

explanation.walkthrough: 'Knows the drill' is an idiom for being experienced, but here drill is literal military exercise; the front is the head of the squad, not the battle line.
explanation.definitionFit: A fugleman was a well-drilled soldier stationed before a company to demonstrate the movements for the others to copy.

clue.text: Pioneer expressman born on Thursday?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: William ..., co-founder of the Wells ... express company
second meaning: the nursery rhyme says Thursday's child has far to go

explanation.walkthrough: The rhyme 'Monday's child' says 'Thursday's child has far to go', so a child born on Thursday must go far.
explanation.definitionFit: William Fargo ran pioneering express delivery services across the American West, so he was an early expressman.

clue.text: Break the law to get riches

indicators.note: to break something is to smash it into a new shape, so the letters are reordered

parts.note: the fodder taken as written

explanation.surface: Crime as a route to getting rich.
explanation.definitionFit: Wealth and riches are synonyms for a great deal of money or possessions.

clue.text: Take French, this should go' without saying!

definitions.text: Take French, this should go' without saying!

parts.note: surface reading: a recommendation to study the French language
setter's reading: taking French ___ means departing without saying goodbye

explanation.walkthrough: To take French leave is to slip away without permission or farewell; 'go without saying' plays on the idiom for something obvious.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word completes the idiom for an unannounced departure, permission to be absent.

clue.text: Pirate announces himself ungrammatically?

indicators.note: announces means speaks out, so the spoken form counts

parts.note: a careless way of saying 'it's me' to identify oneself

explanation.surface: A buccaneer introducing himself in poor English.
explanation.walkthrough: Smee is Captain Hook's bosun in Peter Pan.
explanation.definitionFit: Smee is the famous pirate in J. M. Barrie's Peter Pan, Hook's right-hand man.

clue.text: "For winter's and ruins are over" (Swinburne)

parts.note: surface reading: a line of verse with one word left out
setter's reading: supply the missing word from the chorus in Swinburne's Atalanta in Calydon

explanation.walkthrough: The line runs 'For winter's rains and ruins are over'; the missing word sits after winter's and alliterates with ruins.
explanation.definitionFit: The quotation is incomplete, and only this plural noun for wet weather fills the gap in Swinburne's line.

clue.text: Direct Press, radio, etc, in time-switch

indicators.note: in places one group of letters inside another
a switch is a change of order, so the letters of the word before it are moved about

parts.note: taken as written
the press, radio and television together are the media

explanation.surface: Instructions to a broadcaster about scheduling a switch between press and radio.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Direct' looks like a verb instructing the press, but it is an adjective meaning without delay or intermediary.
explanation.definitionFit: Immediate and direct both describe contact with nothing in between, as in a direct or immediate cause.

clue.text: Decree made once about . faulty drain

indicators.note: about means going round, so one word is wrapped round the other

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: something faulty is out of order, so its letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A council once issued an order about a leaking drain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Once' looks like a time word in the surface, but it is fodder, split so the scrambled drain sits inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: An ordinance is an authoritative order or regulation, which is what a decree is.

clue.text: Products of two on piece work

definitions.text: Products of two on piece work

parts.note: surface reading: paid by the item, the output of two factory hands
setter's reading: musical pieces composed or performed by a pair

explanation.walkthrough: Piece work suggests labour paid by the item, but a piece is also a musical composition worked on by two performers.
explanation.definitionFit: A duet is a musical composition for two performers, so duets are what a pair produces when working on a piece.
